High fever, maculopapular rash, headache,
lymphadenopathy, and inflammatory
polyarthritis.
Arthralgias are more commonly reported (vs

sourceEvidence.claim: SYMPTOMS column — dengue (fever; hemorrhagic fever with plasma leakage; antibodydependent enhancement hyphen-drop; shock syndrome)
sourceEvidence.quote:
Dengue fever: fever, rash, headache, myalgias,
arthralgias, retro-orbital pain, neutropenia.
Dengue hemorrhagic fever: dengue fever +
bleeding and plasma leakage due to severe
thrombocytopenia and RBC perturbations.
Most common if infected with a different
serotype after initial infection due to antibodydependent enhancement of disease.
May progress to dengue shock syndrome:
plasma leakage →  circulatory collapse.

sourceEvidence.claim: Yellow fever block (flavivirus arbovirus; monkey/human reservoir; black vomitus; Councilman bodies; live attenuated vaccine)
sourceEvidence.quote:
Yellow fever virus

A flavivirus (also an arbovirus) transmitted by Aedes mosquito bites. Virus has monkey or human
reservoir. Flavi = yellow, jaundice.
Symptoms: high fever, black vomitus, jaundice, hemorrhage, backache. May see Councilman
bodies (eosinophilic apoptotic globules) on liver biopsy.
Live, attenuated vaccine recommended for travelers to endemic countries.
sourceEvidence.verifiedHow: pdftotext text-layer containment on pinned pages (verify-evidence.ts)

sourceEvidence.claim: Zika block (conjunctivitis; Guillain-Barré; sexual/vertical; congenital Zika syndrome with ventriculomegaly + subcortical calcifications A; microcephaly, ocular, motor)
sourceEvidence.quote:
Zika virus

A flavivirus most commonly transmitted by Aedes mosquito bites.
Causes conjunctivitis, low-grade pyrexia, and itchy rash in 20% of cases. Outbreaks more common
in tropical and subtropical climates. May be complicated by Guillain-Barré syndrome. Supportive
care, no definitive treatment.
Diagnose with RT-PCR or serology.
Sexual and vertical transmission occurs.
In pregnancy, can lead to miscarriage or congenital Zika syndrome: brain imaging shows
ventriculomegaly, subcortical calcifications A . Clinical features in the affected newborn include
▘ Microcephaly
▘ Ocular anomalies
▘ Motor abnormalities (spasticity, seizures)

sourceEvidence.claim: Ebola block, interleaved (filovirus A; 21-day incubation; DIC/hemorrhage/shock; RT-PCR within 48 hr; contact/fomite/bat/primate transmission; supportive; isolation + barrier practices)
sourceEvidence.quote:
A filovirus A . Following an incubation period
of up to 21 days, presents with abrupt onset
of flulike symptoms, diarrhea/vomiting, high
fever, myalgia. Can progress to DIC, diffuse
hemorrhage, shock.
Diagnosed with RT-PCR within 48 hr of
symptom onset. High mortality rate.

Transmission requires direct contact with bodily
fluids, fomites (including dead bodies), infected
bats or primates (apes/monkeys); high incidence
of healthcare-associated infection.
Supportive care, no definitive treatment.
Vaccination of contacts, strict isolation of infected
individuals, and barrier practices for healthcare
workers are key to preventing transmission.

sourceEvidence.claim: SARS-CoV-2 block (⊕ ssRNA; droplets/aerosols/fomites; anosmia/dysgeusia; complications; ▘ NAAT/RAT bullets; spike → ACE2 in lungs-intestines-heart-kidneys; mRNA + viral vector vaccines)
sourceEvidence.quote:
SARS-CoV-2 is a ⊕ ssRNA virus and the cause
of the COVID-19 pandemic. Spread is via
respiratory droplets, aerosols and fomites.
Varying symptoms include: fever, myalgia,
headache, nasal congestion, sneezing, cough,
sore throat, nausea, diarrhea, anosmia,
dysgeusia.
Severe cases may lead to complications like:
pneumonia, hypercoagulability (DVT, PE,
stroke), myocardial injury, neurologic sequelae,
shock, organ failure, death.
Diagnosed by:
▘ NAAT (RT-PCR)
▘ Viral Antigen Test (RAT) →  rapid,
accessible, less sensitive than NAAT

Host cell entry occurs by attachment of viral
spike protein to ACE2 receptor on cell
membranes (highly expressed in the lungs,
intestines, heart, and kidneys).
Vaccines: mRNA and viral vector vaccines
induce immunity by presenting the spike
protein to the immune system leading to antispike protein antibodies.

sourceEvidence.claim: The prion cascade (PrPc α-helical → PrPsc β-pleated; transmissible via CNS tissue iatrogenic CJD or BSE food variant CJD; protease resistance; autocatalysis; autoclave resistance; spongiform encephalopathy — dementia, ataxia, startle myoclonus, death)
sourceEvidence.quote:
Prion diseases are caused by the conversion of a normal (predominantly α-helical) protein termed
prion protein (PrPc) to a β-pleated form (PrPsc), which is transmissible via CNS-related tissue
(iatrogenic CJD) or food contaminated by BSE-infected animal products (variant CJD). PrPsc
resists protease degradation and facilitates the conversion of still more PrPc to PrPsc. Resistant to
standard sterilizing procedures, including standard autoclaving. Accumulation of PrPsc results in
spongiform encephalopathy and dementia, ataxia, startle myoclonus, and death.
sourceEvidence.verifiedHow: pdftotext text-layer containment on pinned pages (verify-evidence.ts)

sourceEvidence.claim: The prion disease trio (CJD sporadic/familial; BSE mad cow; kuru cannibalism)
sourceEvidence.quote:
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease—rapidly progressive dementia, typically sporadic (some familial forms).
Bovine spongiform encephalopathy—also called “mad cow disease.”
Kuru—acquired prion disease noted in tribal populations practicing human cannibalism.
